 Suddenly, Rural Voters Seem Within Reach for Democrats 
 This month, Democrats made gains with rural voters—a long-elusive bloc. What lessons can we draw from Election Day? 
 by 
 Suzanne Mettler 
 November 16, 2026 November 16, 2026

 Democrats made gains with rural voters on Election Day. How can they keep the momentum going? Here, residents from across rural Gunnison County, Colorado at the No Kings Protest, Gunnison, Colorado, March, 2026. Credit: Associated Press 
 For most of the past 30 years, rural Americans have increasingly favored the Republican Party . The Democratic Party, in turn, forfeited votes and power by assuming the gulf was insurmountable. In the 2026 midterms, this divide narrowed, as Americans living in both rural and urban areas voted for change .
 Could the outcome ease our country’s polarization, and spur elected officials to unite and govern for the common good? The answer depends on whether the Democratic Party can turn this month’s electoral victory into a governing coalition that represents cities, suburbs, small towns, and sparsely populated areas, and delivers on citizens’ needs. 
 Many pundits have come to view rural areas as unwinnable for the Democrats, and indeed some party leaders have shared that view, deeming rural America not worth their time or investment. The impression grew that rural voters cared only about culture war issues, or worse, that they were bigots and racists and would never support the party agenda. The evidence does not support those stereotypes , but they prevailed nonetheless.
 On Election Day, both rural and urban Americans signaled that they had had enough. Compared to the 2024 presidential election, both more and less populated places shifted their support to Democratic candidates in U.S. Senate elections. Of the seven seats Democrats flipped in the upper chamber and two more that may flip in Mississippi and Alaska, all but one are in states with a higher percentage of rural residents than the nation. The outlier is Texas, which is only 16 percent rural, but, as the second most populous state, has more rural residents than any other.

 This year’s Democratic candidates won partly by “losing by less” in rural counties, with Democratic Senate candidates gaining more support there than Harris in 2024, helping them secure statewide victories. Yet they also won by outright winning many rural counties that went for Trump two years ago, as did Annie Andrews in South Carolina , James Talarico in Texas , and Roy Cooper in North Carolina .
 The importance of winning Senate seats in low-population states can’t be overstated because the Constitution allocates two seats per state, giving more rural states extra leverage. Historically, each party won some seats in such states, but in recent decades, the Republican Party cemented its power by dominating nearly all of them. That effectively locked the institutional advantage of Senate malapportionment into one party.
 When Republicans control the chamber, as they will until January, they have been elected by only a minority of Americans . This allows them to advance policies opposed by the majority, such as tax cuts for the rich and cuts to social programs, and to confirm judges whose rulings on matters ranging from executive power to abortion and labor law defy public preferences. This year, Democrats broke the GOP hold on the Senate, and in so doing, will permit it to operate by majority rule .

 On the House side, Democrats’ takeover also would not have been so sweeping without increased rural support. In many rural congressional districts, Democrats won outright, with 19 of them projected to flip seats , several of which had been heavily predicted to favor Republicans. The national winds helped, but Democratic candidates still had to overcome decades of distrust. They did that because of impressive credentials, including being rooted in their communities, as well as through tireless campaigning. They include individuals such as Jamie Ager, a fourth-generation farmer and small business owner in the mountains of western North Carolina 11; Sam Forstag, a firefighter with the U.S. Forest Service in his eastern Montana district; and Lindsay James, a Presbyterian minister and state representative in northeastern Iowa, to name a few.
 Republicans’ mid-cycle redistricting efforts missed the mark in rural and more populated districts alike. Two Black Democratic Congressmen from rural districts that were redrawn, Don Davis of North Carolina and Shomari Figures of Alabama, defied the odds and won re-election. They did so thanks to increased Black turnout, perhaps spurred in part by the Trump administration’s attempt to roll back parts of the Voting Rights Act.
 Republicans similarly redrew rural congressional districts in Texas with large Latino populations. Two weeks before the election, I interviewed a Democratic county chair in one of them, TX-23. Four years ago, he told me about the region’s strong support for President Trump and Republican candidates, and that it only deepened in 2024. This year, by contrast, he said, “People are just tired of all the division,” and enthusiastic about the strong Democratic candidates. Indeed, Democrat Katy Padilla Stout flipped that seat; now an attorney, she’s a former kindergarten teacher who had to hide in a closet with 25 kindergartners during the Uvalde school shooting. Similarly, in the TX-15 district, where Democratic candidates ran well before Trump, Bobby Pulido, son of a farmworker and a Tejano musician, returned the seat to Democratic control.
 Democratic victories in rural districts, and narrower losses in others, show that the rural-urban divide is not inevitable, and that a politics that unites Americans regardless of place is possible.
 What happens next? It’s time to build a governing coalition of rural and urban political leaders. Democrats running in rural places—like those in urban places—found that voters were broadly concerned about the economy, with the cost of living and gas prices worsened by the war with Iran; health care, Medicaid, and ACA subsidy cuts; and corruption.   
 Some recent policies harm rural Americans in particular . Tariffs have wreaked havoc in farm states, and multiple candidates I interviewed described heartbreaking conversations with long-time farmers who worried they could not stay in business. In many rural areas, residents faced hospital closures or opposed data center construction.
 If Democrats are to bridge the rural-urban divide, they must understand that rural voters, for the most part, have the same issues on their minds as urban voters, and in some respects, they are particularly vulnerable. Let’s embrace a politics that responds to Americans’ needs regardless of where they live.
